verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster. A song. A psalm. Shout in triumph to God, all [of] the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the leader of the choir, a song, a psalm. Let the whole earth raise the shout, the great ringing cry, for God!
verses.directors_commentary: The verse opens with three labels, and they are working instructions, not decoration: this piece has a leader, it is sung, and it is accompanied. Then comes the order: haria'u, the root of the war cry and the royal acclamation, the noise a crowd makes when a king arrives. KJV's 'make a joyful noise' is pleasant but tame; the verb is closer to a trumpet-blast of loyalty, and the Metzudat David and Malbim both hear it as the shout that greets a king. KJV also writes 'all ye lands' where the Hebrew has the single collective 'all the earth', and it counts the title as verse 0, so the Hebrew verse 1 holds both title and first line. Notice who is addressed: not Israel alone but every land. A director should make the actors project outward, past the walls of the Temple.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative of ru'a, 'to raise a shout': the battle cry, the alarm blast, and the acclamation of a king. It is a loud, public sound, not quiet joy.
A heading found in many psalms, usually taken as 'for the choirmaster/director'. Its precise function is not certain.

verses.translation_literal: Sing praise [to] the glory of his name; set the glory of his praise.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sing out the glory of his name. Give his praise its full weight of glory, and let nothing in it be small.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is built on the word kavod, 'glory', literally 'weight', which appears twice. In the ancient world a name is not a label but a reputation, the whole of what a person is known to be; to sing the weight of the name is to make that reputation public. Hebrew puts kavod first as the thing sung, then as the thing given to the praise itself, and English versions blur this. KJV's 'sing forth the honour of his name: make his praise glorious' keeps the repetition only faintly, and 'honour' and 'glorious' hide that it is one word. Ibn Ezra reads the second half as 'your praise of him is your own honour'. Radak sets the line against the nations' old taunt, 'Where is your God?', so that the song answers an insult. Play it as a deliberate making, not a murmur: the singers are placing glory, piece by piece, like a priest laying out an offering.

philological_notes.note: 'Weight, glory'. It is repeated in both halves, first as the object of the singing and then as what is to be laid on the praise. The English versions render it by two different words.
'Set, place, make'. Ibn Ezra takes it as parallel to 'sing': praise itself becomes the glory.

verses.translation_literal: Say to God: How awesome [are] your deeds! In the greatness of your strength your enemies lie to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: Say to God: how terrible, how wonderful are your deeds! So great is your strength that your very enemies cringe before you and speak with false tongues.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalmist now hands the singers their words: 'Say to God...'. The cry 'mah nora' is an exclamation of awe, and nora, from the root of 'fear', means something that makes you tremble, so KJV's 'terrible' has aged badly in English, where it now just means 'bad'. The real sting is in the second line. The verb yekhachashu comes from kachash, 'to lie, to feign'. The enemies do not simply 'submit themselves' as KJV and ASV have it: they put on a show of obedience because the power in front of them leaves them no choice, and the Hebrew itself has them lying to him. YLT's 'feign obedience' comes closest. Rashi hears the lie confessed under fear; Metzudat David hears enemies pretending to be friends. In the ancient Near East this was exactly how vassals behaved before a great king: a forced loyalty oath, sworn through gritted teeth. Play the line as reluctant, humiliated flattery.

philological_notes.note: From kachash, 'to lie, deny, feign'. Here, enemies feign loyalty or are forced into a false show of submission. English 'submit' is an interpretation; the root means 'to lie'.
A Niphal participle of the root 'to fear': 'to be feared, awesome'. It points to dread and reverence, not 'terrible' in the modern weak sense.

verses.translation_literal: All the earth bow down to you and sing praise to you; they sing praise [to] your name. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: All the earth bows down before you. All the earth sings to you; they sing your name, and the song does not end. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: Having let the enemies lie in verse 3, the psalm now turns to a picture of the whole earth bowing and singing. The verb yishtachavu means to fall down flat, the full prostration of a subject before a ruler, and the psalm is at pains to say that this time the whole earth does it, not only the defeated. KJV makes it a future ('shall worship'), but the Hebrew imperfect can equally be a wish or a certainty, and the shifts between 'to you' and 'your name' give the line a chanting, liturgical rhythm. 'Selah' is a marker whose meaning is no longer known; it may be a pause, a musical lift or an instruction to the instrumentalists, and it is best left unexplained on stage as a held silence. Ibn Ezra notes that 'they sing to you' and 'and they sing to you' are one meaning, said twice.

philological_notes.note: Traditionally taken as a reflexive of shachah, 'to bow down, prostrate oneself': the gesture of homage before a king or a god. KJV's 'worship' is accurate but loses the physical image.
A term of uncertain meaning, probably a musical or liturgical cue (pause, lift, interlude). Meiri reads it here as a call to go on without a break.

verses.translation_literal: Go and see [the] works of God, awesome [in] deed upon [the] sons of Adam.
verses.translation_dramatic: Come, walk out and see what God has done! Awesome is his doing among the children of Adam.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice changes here: the first four verses are a hymn to the nations, and now someone says 'Come and see', the invitation a witness gives to a doubter. It is a pilgrim's call; Ibn Ezra hears one group saying to another 'come to us'. The word 'lekhu' is literally 'go', and in the idiom, 'come on'. The Hebrew for 'works' (mif'alot) and 'deed' (alilah) are two distinct words, the second often used for a doing with a consequence, even a hard one, and KJV's 'he is terrible in his doing toward the children of men' makes the sentence an assertion about God's character that the Hebrew leaves as a plain apposition. Note 'the sons of Adam' where English says 'children of men': it is a bare 'human beings, the earth-creatures', not a male-only phrase, and it sets up the contrast the psalm is about to draw, between what God did for one people and what it means for all.

philological_notes.note: A deed or doing, often one with an effect on others, from the root 'to act upon'. Metzudat Zion links it to ma'alalim, 'deeds, actions'.
Literally 'sons of Adam'; it means 'human beings'. It places the audience of the work in all humanity, not only Israel.

verses.translation_literal: He turned sea to dry land; in the river they pass over on foot; there let us rejoice in him.
verses.translation_dramatic: He turned the sea into dry ground. Through the river they crossed on foot. And there, in that very place, we rejoiced in him.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the heart of the psalm's 'come and see': two crossings folded into one breath. The sea is the Reed Sea of the exodus (Rashi names it), and the river is the Jordan crossed under Joshua, as Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David say. The verb hafakh, 'turned over', is the word for turning a thing upside down, so the sea is not simply parted but overturned into something firm. KJV 'flood' for nahar softens and blurs it: the Hebrew says 'river', and it is the Jordan. The tense shifts too. 'They pass over' is an imperfect, a crossing seen unrolling, and then the singer steps into the scene with a cohortative: 'there let us rejoice'. KJV 'did we rejoice' makes this a flat past, but the Hebrew is the singer's own voice, generations later, standing on the shore as if the worshipper were there. Let the actor move from telling to being there.

philological_notes.note: 'To turn over, overturn', the word used of the overthrow of Sodom. Here the sea itself is turned into dry land.
A first person plural cohortative ('let us rejoice'), which makes the singers present at the crossing. KJV and ASV flatten it to the past.

verses.translation_literal: Ruling by his might forever, his eyes on the nations keep watch; the rebellious, let them not exalt themselves. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: He rules by his might, forever. His eyes keep watch over the nations, and they do not close. Let the rebels not lift up their heads. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: From the past the psalm moves to the present tense of kingship. 'Moshel' is a participle, a ruler ruling, and 'olam' is 'for all time' or 'to the age'. The picture of eyes that 'keep watch' is the watchman on the wall, the same verb as the lookout: tzafah. KJV's 'behold' is gentler and passive, where the Hebrew eyes are on guard duty. The last clause is a prohibition aimed at the 'sorerim', the stubborn, the ones who turn aside; the ancient word is used of a stubborn and rebellious son in Deuteronomy, so this is a household word for obstinacy and not an abstract 'rebel'. A literal 'do not lift themselves up' keeps the physical image of a head raised in pride, and Rashi glosses it as 'let their hand not be high'. There is a Qere marked on the verb. Play it as a warning issued gently, from a king who does not need to raise his voice.

philological_notes.note: 'To keep watch, look out'. Used of a sentry. The feminine plural verb agrees with 'eyes'.
'The stubborn, rebellious ones', from sarar, 'to turn aside, be obstinate'. Metzudat David glosses it as those who turn from the way of good.

verses.translation_literal: Bless, peoples, our God, and make heard [the] sound of his praise.
verses.translation_dramatic: Bless our God, you peoples! Let the sound of his praise be heard, and let it carry far.
verses.directors_commentary: The first half of the psalm ends with a new, broader summons: not 'all the earth' this time but 'amim', peoples, and the pronoun shifts to 'our God', the first sign that the singer speaks as one of a particular community, and that the others are being invited into that community's God. This is a quiet, large claim: the god of one people is asked to be blessed by all. 'Bless' is barukh, the verb used of a blessing in prayer, usually directed from a lesser to a greater, so it reads as an act of homage and not as a favour. Ibn Ezra notes a tradition that 'amim' here means Israel's own tribes, as in Benjamin's 'among your peoples', but the plain reading is the nations. KJV's 'the voice of his praise' keeps the Hebrew 'kol', but 'sound' makes the point plainer: the praise is a noise to be broadcast, not a private feeling. Let the actor turn from the audience to the whole horizon.

philological_notes.note: 'Peoples'. Ibn Ezra records the view that here it means Israel's own tribes, and prefers it; the plain sense is the other nations.
Hiphil of shama', 'to cause to be heard', the same pattern as 'make a sound public', which is why KJV writes 'make... to be heard'.

verses.translation_literal: The [one] placing our soul in life, and he has not given our foot to slipping.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the one who set our very breath among the living, and he did not let our feet slip.
verses.directors_commentary: A pair of images from daily life: the 'nefesh' placed 'in life', and the foot that is not 'given to slipping'. Nefesh is not the later English 'soul' but the whole living self, the throat, the breath, the appetite of a person; to 'place' it 'in life' is to put the creature among the living and keep it there. KJV 'holdeth our soul in life' is fair, though 'holdeth' is a little static for the verb sam, 'to set'. The second line is the mountain-path image: mot is a stumble or sway, as when a foot gives way on a stony slope, and in a land of cliffs and wadis a stumble could be fatal. KJV 'suffereth not our feet to be moved' is old English for 'does not allow'. Radak and Metzudat David both read it as survival through exile; Malbim, as keeping the people from turning away. Say it with the relief of someone who has just crossed a dangerous ridge.

philological_notes.note: 'Our life, our self, our throat'. Usually translated 'soul', but it means the whole living person.
'To slipping, stumbling, being shaken'. Metzudat Zion links it to the sense of swaying or tilting of the foot.

verses.translation_literal: For you have tested us, God; you have refined us as the refining of silver.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you tested us, O God. You put us through the fire and refined us, as a smith refines silver.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the pivot of the psalm. The earlier verses sang of victory; this one admits that the victory came through pain, and it names God as the one who sent it. The metaphor is the silversmith's: the metal is heated in the crucible until the dross rises and can be skimmed off. In the ancient world silver was the standard of wealth, and refining it was a skilled, hot, wasteful work, where some of the metal was lost as well. The Hebrew repeats the root twice, 'you refined us as the refining of silver' (tzerafttanu kitzrof), a wordplay that KJV's 'tried us as silver is tried' loses by swapping 'refine' for 'try'. Rashi and Metzudat David both read the refining as the removal of sin through suffering; Ibn Ezra reads 'test' as a figure, since nothing is hidden from God anyway. Let the actor hold the heat in the voice: this is gratitude and grievance together.

philological_notes.note: A figura etymologica: the verb and the noun 'refining' share the root. It is the smelter's image of heating silver to separate the dross.
'To test, examine'. Ibn Ezra stresses that this is a figure of speech, since the hidden things of the heart are already known to God.

verses.translation_literal: You brought us into the net; you put a crushing burden on our loins.
verses.translation_dramatic: You brought us into the net, and it closed. You laid a crushing weight on our loins, until we could not stand straight.
verses.directors_commentary: Two hunting and labouring images pile up. The 'metzudah' is a net or snare, the trapper's tool, and it can also mean a stronghold, which is why Rashi and Metzudat Zion hear a prison or a walled fortress; the net image is the plain one. The 'mu'akah' is a pressing, squeezing weight, from the root that means 'to press down', the same family as Amos' cart pressed down with sheaves. It is set 'on the loins', literally the hips, the seat of strength and the place where a worker's belt is tied; to have the burden there is to be bent double. KJV 'loins' is right and keeps the anatomical word; BBE's 'chains put on our legs' is a paraphrase and not the Hebrew at all. Meiri hears a belt pulled too tight, Malbim an iron band. The voice drops: this is an admission, said close to the ground.

philological_notes.note: 'Net, snare' (a hunter's trap), and also 'stronghold'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as a confining place, a prison or fort.
'A pressing burden', related to the verb 'to press' in Amos 2:13. The sense is a constriction around the hips.

verses.translation_literal: You made a man ride at our head; we came into fire and into water, and you brought us out to saturation.
verses.translation_dramatic: You let mortal men ride over our heads. We went into fire, we went into water, and then you brought us out into a place of overflowing plenty.
verses.directors_commentary: The images of ordeal keep coming. 'You made a man ride at our head' pictures a charioteer or horseman trampling over the people; the word is enosh, a frail mortal, set against the God who allowed it. KJV 'men' is plural, the Hebrew is a singular collective, and Rashi reads it as the kings of every nation. Fire and water are the two ancient dangers, burning and flooding, and both ended in escape, as the psalm says at last. The final word, revayah, comes from the root of 'being drenched with water', the opposite of a dry land: the people leave an ordeal of fire and flood for a land well watered. KJV 'a wealthy place' is a guess at an unusual word; Ibn Ezra, by contrast, wants 'open air', and Radak has the land of Israel itself. The line is the emotional turn of the psalm, from the narrow place to the open, and the actor should let the breath widen on the last word.

philological_notes.note: 'Saturation, abundance', from the root 'to be watered, drunk full'. Many take it as a well-watered, fertile place. KJV 'wealthy place' is a guess.
'A man, a mortal', the word that stresses human frailty. Rashi reads the single man as the kings of each nation.

verses.translation_literal: I will come [to] your house with burnt offerings; I will pay to you my vows,
verses.translation_dramatic: I will come into your house, and I will not come empty-handed: the smoke of the burnt offerings will go before me. All that I promised, I will pay you in full.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play the turn here: for twelve verses the voice was a crowd, 'we', and now one person steps out of it and walks toward the Temple. Rashi, Radak and Meiri hear the whole people speaking in the singular; a performer can let the actor start alone and let the choir hear itself in him. The 'house' is the sanctuary, and the 'burnt offering' (olah) is the offering that goes wholly up in smoke, with no meal for the worshiper, so the gift is a costly one.

The verb 'pay' (shalem) is the language of debts, and the vow (neder) is exactly that: a promise made in a bad hour, 'if you rescue me, I will give you...', that now comes due. KJV's 'I will go into thy house' is acceptable, though the Hebrew verb is the plain 'come, enter'; the Hebrew has no preposition before 'house', which the KJV supplies. 'Pay thee my vows' is faithful, and BBE's 'my debt' flattens the plural, since the speaker owes several vows.

philological_notes.note: Piel of the root of shalom, 'wholeness': to make complete, to settle a debt. Paying a vow restores the balance between the worshiper and God.
A conditional promise to God made in distress, to be paid when the distress is relieved; the next verse names the circumstance. Rashi reads these as vows made in exile.

verses.translation_literal: which my lips opened, and my mouth spoke, in distress to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: The vows my lips tore open to speak, the words my mouth gave you when the walls were closing in on me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The vows were not made in comfort. 'Distress' (tsar) comes from the root for narrowness, a tight place, and the actor should hear it: the promises were squeezed out of him when he had no room to move. 'Opened my lips' is a pointed picture, since the lips were shut with fear and the promise forced them apart (Ibn Ezra compares Judges 11:35, 'I have opened my mouth to the LORD').

KJV 'uttered' and 'hath spoken' blur two separate things: lips that opened and a mouth that spoke, the same parallelism the Hebrew keeps. KJV also ends 'when I was in trouble', which turns the noun 'in the narrow place to me' into a mild past tense. The Hebrew is more physical and more intimate: the narrowness was his own.

philological_notes.note: To open wide, usually the mouth. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'opened'; used of a vow as in Judges 11:35-36.
Literally 'in the narrow [place] to me', a frequent idiom for distress. Radak ties it to the moment the enemy pressed upon the exiles.

verses.translation_literal: Burnt offerings of fatlings I will offer up to you, with the smoke of rams; I will make cattle with goats. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Fat young animals, whole upon the altar, I will send up to you, and the rams' smoke climbing with them. Oxen I will bring, and goats beside them. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a list meant to be heard as abundance: fatlings, rams, bulls, he-goats, the four great animals of the ancient altar. The wealth is staggering for a vow-payer, since a bull cost many months of a farmer's income; this is the offering of someone who has been brought back from the edge. The speaker is likely a king or a community speaking in one voice, since few private persons could pay this.

'Fatlings' (mechim) is related to the word for marrow, 'mo'ach'; Rashi and Radak read it as animals rich in marrow and fat. KJV's 'incense of rams' is a mistranslation: qeṭoret is the rising smoke, and Radak and Metzudat David say it is the burning of the rams' fat parts on the altar, so it is meat, not spice. 'I will make' bulls is the idiom for preparing and offering a sacrifice; KJV 'offer' covers it, but note that the Hebrew uses two verbs, 'offer up' (alah) and 'make' (asah). Selah closes the section with a pause whose meaning is lost to us.

philological_notes.note: Fatlings, animals well filled with marrow; Rashi and Radak connect it to the word for marrow.
From the root 'to make smoke'. Here it is the smoke of burning fat, not an aromatic mixture; KJV 'incense' misleads.
A musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning, probably a pause or lifting. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'truly'; Metzudat David as 'forever'.

verses.translation_literal: Come, hear, and let me recount, all fearers of God, what he has done for my soul.
verses.translation_dramatic: Come, all of you who stand in awe of God, come close and listen. Let me tell you what he has done for me, for my very life.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood shifts from the altar to the courtyard. The speaker turns and speaks to the crowd, and the actor should open his arms to them. 'Come' (lekhu) is an urgent summons, as Radak and Meiri note, a call to hurry, not a polite invitation. 'Fearers of God' is a recognized group in the ancient world: those who revere him. Rashi reads them as proselytes; most others take it as the faithful of Israel.

KJV 'my soul' keeps the Hebrew nefesh but modern ears hear a spiritual part. Here nefesh is the whole living self, throat and breath, the life that was in the narrow place. 'Declare' for 'recount' (saphar) is acceptable, but the verb is the one for counting: he is going to tell the story item by item.

philological_notes.note: Not 'soul' in the later sense: the person, the life, the throat. 'For my soul' means 'for me, for my life'.
'Those who fear God', the reverent. Rashi reads them as converts who join Israel.

verses.translation_literal: To him my mouth I called, and exaltation [was] under my tongue.
verses.translation_dramatic: I called to him with my own mouth, and already, under my tongue, the praise was waiting.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two pictures: a cry going out, and praise held ready under the tongue. The Hebrew word order puts 'to him' first, so the shout was aimed at God and no one else. 'Under the tongue' is a picture of something kept in reserve, as a sweet is held in the mouth (Rashi compares Job 20:12, where wickedness is hidden 'under his tongue'); here the opposite is hidden, praise held ready until the rescue came. Malbim's reading, from the sages, is that the speaker first cried to every idol and then to the LORD.

The second half is read two ways. The STEPBible tagging and Rashi's second gloss take romam as a noun, 'exaltation (of him)', which makes the clause verbless and pictorial; this is the literal layer. Radak and Rashi's first gloss take it as a verb: 'I exalted him with my tongue', 'he was exalted'. KJV's 'he was extolled with my tongue' follows that verbal reading, and it is a defensible one, though it loses the 'under' of the Hebrew and shifts the focus from the praise held ready to the act of praising. BBE's 'I was lifted up from the underworld' has nothing behind it in the Hebrew.

philological_notes.note: Read two ways. As a noun, 'exaltation' (STEPBible, Rashi's second gloss): 'his exaltation is ready under my tongue'. As a verb, 'I exalted him' or 'he was exalted' (Radak, Rashi's first gloss, and KJV and ASV). The literal layer keeps the noun.
'Under my tongue': the place where speech is ready but not yet spoken. Radak takes it as 'on my tongue'.

verses.translation_literal: Wickedness, if I had seen [it] in my heart, the Lord would not listen.
verses.translation_dramatic: If I had cherished wrong in my heart, the Lord would never have listened.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm, and it can be played two ways. The first, the common one: a prayer is only heard when the heart is clean, so the speaker is saying 'I came with nothing hidden'. The second is Malbim's: 'seeing' wickedness in the heart is a doubt that God hears at all. The director must choose, and the dramatic layer chooses the first.

The verb 'saw' (ra'iti) is an odd one. English 'regard' in KJV comes close, a look that lingers, as when one holds a thing dear. But the word order puts 'wickedness' first, as a thing set before the eye: the Hebrew is blunter than KJV's soft opening 'If I regard iniquity'. BBE's 'I said in my heart' invents a speech. Note also the shift from 'God' (Elohim) to 'Lord' (Adonai), a title of mastery that fits a servant's plea. Radak and Meiri add a legal note: evil thought alone is not counted as an act.

philological_notes.note: Wickedness, trouble, emptiness; a general word for crooked intent, often tied to idolatry.
'I saw', that is looked upon and held; English 'regard' fits, 'I found' is also possible. Malbim understands it as admitting doubt.

verses.translation_literal: Surely God has heard; he has paid attention to the sound of my prayer.
verses.translation_dramatic: But he did hear! God heard, he leaned in and listened to the voice of my prayer.
verses.directors_commentary:
Release after the tension of the last verse: akhen, 'but truly', is the word of a man who has just been proved right against his own fear. Play it as a breath let go. The verbs come in a pair, 'heard' and 'attended', and the second (hiqshiv) is the stronger, the picture of leaning the ear toward a sound, or pricking it up.

KJV 'verily' is archaic but sound; 'hath heard me' adds a pronoun the Hebrew lacks, and the ASV is closer. Notice that what God heard is the 'sound' (qol) of the prayer, its voice, not its words: he responds to the cry itself. Malbim adds that the hearing came the moment the prayer began.

philological_notes.note: 'Surely, but truly': an assertion that sets a fact against a doubt. Rashi: 'in truth, it must be known'.
Hiphil, to cause the ear to attend: to listen closely, to give heed.

verses.translation_literal: Blessed [be] God, who has not turned aside my prayer, or his covenant loyalty from me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed be God, who did not push my prayer away, and who has not taken his faithful love from me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends its personal section on a blessing, and the closing note is generous: what God did not remove was both the prayer and his hesed. Hesed is the loyal love owed within a covenant, and the speaker is amazed that he has been kept inside the bond. Metzudat David and Malbim take it as grace: God could have refused him on his record and did not.

The verb 'turn aside' (hesir) is the same used for taking away a thing set before one; Radak says the prayer was not pushed back, but received with favor. KJV's 'mercy' and its 'nor his mercy from me' are not wrong, but hesed is not mercy toward a stranger; it is the faithfulness of a covenant partner. KJV also joins the two halves with 'nor', which the Hebrew does with a plain 'and'. BBE reverses the grammar, making 'good faith and mercy' the thing taken away. The verse ends on 'from me', so the last sound is the fear of loss, answered.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, faithful love: the obligation of the stronger partner to the weaker. KJV 'mercy' is too thin.
Hiphil, to cause to turn aside, to remove; Radak reads it as God not dismissing the prayer.
